title: I Enforced the Soup-Kitchen Hairnet Log on the Shift Lead Who Skipped It

parts.text: I clocked the serving line at 11:08 a.m. and shift lead Donna was plating without a hairnet while the clipboard said: NET ON. INITIAL THE LOG. LEADS FIRST. I was fifty-two, volunteer, holding a boxed net. Donna waved a ladle. "Leads are the line." I photographed the uncovered hair, the clipboard, and the empty initial box. Then I logged a skip. At 11:16 the kitchen manager asked why Donna's hair was on an unsigned log. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The kitchen manager can see Donna plating without a net against the initial box.

social.video_title: The shift lead plated without initialing the hairnet log — Part 1/2
social.description: Soup kitchen, a boxed net, and a clipboard the lead posted. I logged the skip. Would you have photographed the hair?

parts.text: Donna called it steam until the manager asked for the log. I printed the skip, the photo, and the clipboard. She netted. Donna initialed first and told volunteers steam was always about optics. Optics is a word leads use when hair exists. Hairnet policy now has a second line: LEADS NET. I keep the log. Donna initials. The line finally looks like a kitchen, not a shortcut. I kept the printout in a folder labeled BORING. I have learned the difference between a title and a line item.

social.description: Skip log, netted lead, and a second line. Was steam ever an empty initial box?
